items.prompt: Suggest a sustainable water-use response for an invented settlement where garden pumping during a dry period leaves insufficient water for essential household needs. Explain why it fits this problem.
items.canonical_answer: Agree a monitored allocation that reserves essential household water and limits garden pumping, while repairing avoidable leaks. This addresses current needs and reduces the risk of exhausting the available supply.
marking_guidance: Context: respond to competition between the garden and essential household access.
Reason: explain how the proposed allocation or reduced waste protects both present needs and future supply; accept another feasible matched response.

items.prompt: Suggest a conservation measure for an invented woodland where trees are cut faster than they regrow. Explain why it fits a renewable resource.
items.canonical_answer: Limit cutting to a monitored level compatible with regeneration and protect young trees. This gives regrowth an opportunity to replace losses rather than assuming renewability prevents depletion.
marking_guidance: Context: address excessive cutting relative to regrowth.
Reason: connect the measure to regeneration; planting without changing excessive extraction is not sufficient by itself.

items.prompt: Explain the likely change in an invented woodland if 160 trees are cut but 100 replace losses annually, and those rates persist.
items.canonical_answer: The woodland loses a net 60 trees per year. Extraction exceeds replacement, so the stock declines despite the resource being renewable and may become less able to support future use.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: link extraction above replacement to a falling stock, using both supplied rates.
Consequence: connect net loss of 60 trees to reduced future availability.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Explain the error in saying: “Wood is renewable, so limiting tree cutting is unnecessary.”
items.canonical_answer: Renewable means it can regenerate on a human timescale under suitable conditions, not that its stock cannot fall. Test whether cutting exceeds regrowth: if it does, conservation is needed to maintain the stock.
marking_guidance: Error: treating renewability as immunity to depletion.
Distinction: regeneration versus a finite non-renewable stock; use the cutting-versus-regrowth test.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Explain the error in defining sustainable development solely as farming that protects soil.
items.canonical_answer: Soil-protecting farming is an example of sustainable agriculture. Sustainable development is broader and includes other activities that meet present needs while protecting future needs; test whether the statement concerns farming specifically or the wider principle.
marking_guidance: Error: a farming-specific application is substituted for the broader concept.
Distinction: sustainable agriculture versus sustainable development, with a farming-specific versus wider-principle test.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Discuss whether an invented school should replace 200 single-use cups a week with durable cups to reduce discarded material. It has storage and a safe washing arrangement, but must pay an initial purchase cost.
items.canonical_answer: Durable cups are a reasonable choice for the stated waste aim because repeated use can replace a continuing flow of discarded cups, and storage and safe washing are available. The initial cost and maintenance remain drawbacks. Adoption is justified if the purchase is affordable and cups are repeatedly used rather than quickly lost or discarded.
marking_guidance: Judgement: support a choice against the waste-reduction aim.
Reason: weigh repeated-use benefits against the supplied initial cost and practical washing/storage conditions. A supported conditional decision is valid.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Suggest one responsible-production response for a fictional tailoring group that discards usable fabric offcuts while buying new fabric for small bags. Explain one resource-saving benefit and name one Sustainable Development Goal directly supported by the action.
items.canonical_answer: Sort suitable offcuts and use them for the small bags. This reduces the new fabric required and the usable fabric discarded, provided the pieces fit the required bag sizes. It directly supports SDG 12, Responsible Consumption and Production.
marking_guidance: Context, 1 mark: a feasible reuse response addressing the offcuts and small bags.
Reason, 1 mark: connect that response to reduced new-material use or avoidable waste; do not count the same benefit twice.
Goal, 1 mark: identify SDG 12 or its title, Responsible Consumption and Production. No paid-work assumption or second goal is required.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: State (a) two pillars of sustainable development [2]. Explain (b) why an invented woodland’s renewability does not establish that its use is sustainable when 90 trees regenerate but 130 are cut annually, with rates otherwise unchanged [4].
items.canonical_answer: (a) Any two of the economic, social and environmental pillars. (b) Cutting 130 trees while only 90 regenerate gives a net loss of 40 trees annually. If the rates persist, the woodland stock declines despite the resource being renewable. That decline can reduce resources available for future users. Limiting extraction and protecting regeneration addresses this mechanism; the renewable label alone does not establish sustainable use.
marking_guidance: Point (a), 2 marks: name any two distinct pillars from economic, social and environmental; one mark for each.

Development (b), up to 4 marks: compare extraction with regeneration, establish the declining stock, connect it to future needs and explain a matched response or condition. A definition without application is insufficient.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Describe (a) the resource-use relationship in this original fictional table for the same output of 100 bags: Method A uses 25 metres of new fabric and discards 5 metres; Method B uses 20 metres and discards 1 metre [3]. Suggest (b) which method a group should adopt if its aim is to reduce new-fabric use and waste; both methods meet the same quality standard and require the same available skills [3].
items.canonical_answer: (a) B produces the same output using 5 metres less new fabric and discarding 4 metres less. Lower new-input use accompanies less waste. (b) Choose B for the stated aim: it reduces both new-fabric demand and discarded material without changing the required output, quality or skill availability. The conclusion is confined to the stated criteria.
marking_guidance: Evidence (a), up to 3 marks: compare input and discarded amounts for equal output and infer the resource-efficiency relationship.
Meaning (b), up to 3 marks: a supported choice linked to both criteria and the supplied feasibility facts. Do not invent a price saving or unprovided environmental effect.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.
